titleEn: Scald Burn - Cooling, BSA and Analgesia

patient.name: Jordan Hayes
patient.affectEn: alert, grimacing and swearing under his breath with pain; standing at the double sink holding his right arm and chest under the cool running tap water; does not want to leave the water because the burning is worse when it stops
patient.speechEn: speaks in full sentences, clear normal voice; cooperative; answers questions directly but keeps coming back to how much it burns

scene.settingEn: Commercial kitchen of a restaurant in Langley at 1150 hrs. The burner is off and the stockpot lies on the floor, its contents spilled; the floor is wet. The patient stands at a double sink with his right arm and chest under cool running tap water while a coworker helps him. The kitchen is hot, about 30 degrees C. No smoke, no fire, not an enclosed space. One patient.
hazardsEn: wet floor from the spilled stockpot - slip hazard
hot kitchen surfaces and hot liquids (burner now off)
no smoke, no fire, no enclosed-space exposure

bystanders.knowsEn: saw the stockpot handle slip as he carried the boiling water to the sink; the water went over his right arm and chest; put him straight under the cool tap and he has been there ever since; he did not fall or pass out; no fire or smoke; will help hold the arm under the water, fetch blankets or hold doors if asked
nothing beyond what the coworker says; called 911; can clear the floor or fetch things under your direction

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: sterile non-stick dry gauze and burn dressings
sterile normal saline (for cooling if running water is not available)
Entonox cylinder with demand valve and mouthpiece
oxygen kit with nasal cannula and non-rebreather mask
PCP only: oral analgesia kit (acetaminophen and ibuprofen tablets)
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline

dispatchEn: 1150 hrs. Code 3 to a commercial kitchen in a Langley restaurant. 29-year-old male tipped a stockpot of boiling water onto his right arm and chest. Staff have him at the sink. Hospital is 12 minutes away; the burn unit is at a tertiary centre 40 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: staff put him under cool running water immediately and he has been there about 4 minutes. He is conscious and talking.
arrivalEn: A cook waves you through the dining room into the kitchen. The burner is off and a stockpot lies on its side on the wet floor. The kitchen is hot, about 30 degrees C. The patient stands at the double sink with his right arm and chest under cool running tap water, a coworker beside him. No smoke, no fire, not an enclosed space. One patient.
firstLookEn: An alert 29-year-old man standing at the sink, grimacing and swearing under his breath, holding his right arm and chest under the running water. His right arm and the front of his chest are red and blistered. No soot on his face, no singed hair.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU = A). Grimacing with pain, speaks in full sentences, answers appropriately.
primary.airwayEn: Clear. Voice normal - no hoarseness, no stridor. No soot in the mouth or nose, no singed nasal hair, no facial burn.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 108, strong and regular. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: When exposed: a partial-thickness burn - red, blistered, wet and extremely painful - over the ENTIRE right upper limb, front and back, and over the anterior chest. No circumferential full-thickness burn, no full-thickness area, no involvement of the hands, face or groin. He is still wearing his wet shirt and a wristwatch. Rest of the RBS: no other injuries - head, neck, abdomen, pelvis, back, both legs and the left arm are unremarkable. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: unburned skin pink, warm and dry. Scald only - no fall, c-spine not indicated. If the candidate takes him away from the running water: "It's way worse when the water stops!"

history.ccEn: My arm and my chest - the boiling water went all over me. It's burning like crazy.

opqrst.oEn: About six minutes before you got here. I was carrying a stockpot of boiling water to the sink, the handle slipped and it went over my right arm and my chest. My coworker put me straight under the tap.
opqrst.pEn: The cool water helps. It's way worse when the water stops.
opqrst.rEn: Just my right arm and my chest. It doesn't go anywhere else.

history.painScoreEn: 9 out of 10. (Once analgesia - Entonox, or the oral analgesics - has been given and has had time to work: 4 out of 10.)

sample.sEn: My arm and chest are burning. That's it - I'm breathing fine and my throat feels fine.
sample.aEn: No allergies that I know of.
sample.lEn: Staff lunch at eleven, about an hour ago.
sample.eEn: I was carrying the stockpot of boiling water to the sink and the handle slipped. The water went over my right arm and chest. I didn't fall and I didn't black out. No fire, no smoke - it was just the water, and the kitchen isn't closed in.

fe.generalEn: I'm fit. I work full-time here.
fe.respiratoryEn: No cough, I'm not short of breath, and my throat feels fine - no irritation.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart's racing - it's the pain.
fe.giGuEn: Nothing there. I haven't thrown up.
fe.integumentaryEn: Just the burn on my arm and chest. (After several minutes of cooling: "I'm starting to shiver.")
fe.musculoskeletalEn: No other injuries. Nothing else hurts.
fe.eentEn: Nothing splashed in my eyes, my face is fine, and my voice is normal.

findings.headNeckEn: No burns, no soot, no singed nasal hair. Voice clear, no stridor.
findings.chestLungsEn: Partial-thickness burn over the whole anterior chest: red, blistered, wet. Air entry equal and clear at all 6 sites.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Unburned. Circulation, sensation and movement intact.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: RIGHT arm: partial-thickness burn of the entire limb, front and back; circumferentially reddened but NOT a full circumferential burn; blisters intact; radial pulse present, sensation intact, fingers move. LEFT arm: normal.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: after cooling, dressing and analgesia; if no analgesic is ever given set 1 stays current
vitalsSets.skin: unburned areas pink, warm, dry; mild shivering settling under blankets

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The patient has started to shiver.

expected.actionEn: Complete 15-20 minutes of cooling with cool running water, counting bystander time, without over-cooling the patient
Dress with sterile non-stick DRY gauze only after cooling; do not break blisters or apply creams or ice
Run the Pain Management protocol with contraindications ruled out for each drug

Prevent hypothermia: cover unburned areas, warm ambulance, monitor temperature

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate applies the dressing to the burn (the act itself - not a statement that they will dress it after cooling)
candidate applies ice, ice packs, cold packs or ice-cold water to the burn (an actual application - saying that ice must not be used is NOT this event)

candidate continues active cooling well past 20 minutes in total - counting the staff's cooling that began right after the injury, about 6 minutes before your arrival - or wets and cools large unburned areas of the body

candidate stops the cooling early in order to dress the burn, or applies the dressing before about 15 minutes of total cooling (counting the staff's cooling that began about 6 minutes before your arrival)
candidate puts a wet or soaked dressing, a cream, ointment, gel, butter or any other substance on the burn instead of a dry sterile non-stick dressing
candidate breaks, pops, drains or deroofs the blisters

candidate administers a medication without having asked about or examined for that medication's contraindications at any earlier point in the call (Entonox: inhalation injury, altered LOC, pneumothorax, ability to comply; acetaminophen: liver disease, acetaminophen taken in the past 4 hours; ibuprofen: active GI bleed or ulcer, anticoagulants, NSAID allergy). The standard history (medical history, medications, allergies) and the airway check for inhalation injury count when they were done earlier.
PCP gives a fluid bolus (runs normal saline wide open or orders a set volume such as 20 mL/kg or 500 mL); starting an IV with saline at TKVO is NOT this event

drugs.doseEn: Inhalation, self-administered through the demand valve; titrate to effect; invert the cylinder 3 times before use. Indicated for pain associated with burns; contraindicated with inhalation injury or altered LOC (none here). Only after the primary survey, the pain assessment including severity, and baseline vitals including SpO2.
1000 mg PO (guideline range 500-1000 mg PO; may repeat once after 4 hours - not within 4 hours of any previous dose)
400 mg PO (guideline range 300-400 mg PO; may repeat every 4-6 hours)

IV only if indicated; a fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L is for hypotension or burns over 20% BSA - NOT indicated at 18% with a normal blood pressure. (Cool sterile saline on the burn for cooling is not this drug.)

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You exposed the patient during your rapid body survey - what did you find on his arm and chest?

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR: cooling, BSA calculation, dry sterile non-stick dressings, hypothermia prevention and Entonox for analgesia are all EMR-level. EMR does not give oral analgesics or establish IV access. No Functional Enquiry. Appendix A: Entonox is indicated for pain associated with burns - omitting it costs 25%, and omitting it while dressing the burn is treated like realigning without analgesia (100%).
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds acetaminophen and ibuprofen to the analgesia ladder and the 9-system Functional Enquiry. IV fluid is only indicated for burns over 20% BSA or hypotension - at 18% with normal blood pressure a fluid bolus is NOT indicated, and giving one is a non-indicated intervention. Appendix A applies: acetaminophen and ibuprofen without Entonox is 25%; Entonox delayed until after the dressing is applied is up to 100%.

sourcePages: Scenario tr-05 (data/practical/scenarios.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (Burn Management and Pain Management), ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (major burns: partial thickness > 20% BSA, full thickness > 10%, facial or airway burns, burns that fully encircle a limb - 18% partial thickness with none of these is stable); p.11 Primary survey interventions (initiating cooling of burns; oxygen indications); p.28 Burn Management (expose and examine; initiate cooling for 15-20 minutes inclusive of bystander cooling, with cool not cold running water; high-flow oxygen only for suspected inhalation injury or SOB; calculate BSA by the Rule of Nines; consider pain management; once cooling has finished dress with sterile, nonstick, dry gauze; PCP IV if indicated, hypotensive 20 ml/kg to a maximum of 2 litres); p.35 (do not cool burns longer than 15-20 minutes); p.54 Hypovolemia (indication includes burns > 20% BSA); p.58 Acetaminophen (500-1,000 mg PO, not within 4 hours of a previous dose); p.65 Entonox (indication: pain associated with burns; contraindications incl. inhalation injury and altered LOC; before use: primary survey, pain complaint incl. severity, baseline vitals incl. SpO2, history and physical to rule out contraindications; invert cylinder 3 X); p.68 Ibuprofen (300-400 mg PO; contraindications incl. active GI hemorrhage or ulcers and anticoagulants); EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria Appendix A (Pain Management weighting, as in tr-01).
